lessons.title: Observational drawing: shading techniques
objectives: Draw a piece of fruit by looking carefully
Describe tone using the words light, mid and dark

keywords.def: to look very carefully before drawing
shading with lines that go in one direction
shading with lines that cross each other

starter: Bismillah. What is tone? Give an example.
Name two shapes in a mosque skyline.
How do you make a dark mark with a pencil?

teach.heading: Looking before drawing
bullets: Look at the outline and the shadows
Allah created every detail to notice
teach.note: Pupils need a pencil, paper and a piece of fruit (apple or orange). Say bismillah. Ask pupils to look for 30 seconds before touching the pencil.

teach.heading: Three shading techniques
teach.note: Draw each in a box on screen. Misconception: more pressure is the only way to get dark; closer lines make dark too.

teach.heading: Drawing the outline
bullets: Start with a light pencil outline
Check the shape against the fruit
teach.note: Model a light outline. Teach 'draw what you see, not what you think you see'.

teach.heading: Adding tone
bullets: Find where the light comes from
Shade the side away from light
teach.note: Place a lamp or window on one side. Ask: which side is darkest? Model shading with hatching.

teach.heading: Reviewing our drawing
bullets: Is there a light, mid and dark?
teach.note: Show 2 examples and ask for a kind, specific comment.

practice: Draw a box and fill it with hatching.
Draw a box and fill it with stippling.
independent: Draw a hatching strip, a cross-hatching strip and a stippling strip.
Shade a circle to look like a ball using one technique.
exit: Draw an apple using hatching or stippling to show tone.
Write one sentence about which technique you like best and why.
homework: Which side of the fruit is darkest?
lessons.send: Draw a piece of fruit from your kitchen using one shading technique.

lessons.title: Islamic geometric patterns: the six-petal flower
objectives: Describe what makes a geometric pattern
Construct a six-petal flower with a compass or string
Colour the pattern with a limited palette

keywords.def: using shapes and lines drawn with measuring tools
a tool for drawing circles and arcs
the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge
when one half is a mirror image of the other

starter: What is the radius of a circle?

teach.heading: Patterns in Islamic art
bullets: Islamic art uses repeating geometric shapes
Many mosques and books use them
teach.note: Show photos of tiles or book decoration on screen. Mention these designs avoid pictures of living things and focus on shapes and order. Pupils need paper, pencil, ruler and a compass (or a pencil tied to string with a grown-up's help).

teach.heading: Drawing the circle
bullets: Place the compass point in the centre
Do not change the compass width
teach.note: Demonstrate slowly. Misconception: changing the width. Tell pupils to keep it fixed, perhaps wrapping tape on the compass.

teach.heading: Marking six points
bullets: Put the point anywhere on the circle
Draw a small arc across the circle
Move to the new point and repeat
teach.note: Step round the circle six times; the sixth mark lands back on the start. This works because the radius fits around a circle exactly six times.

teach.heading: Drawing the petals
bullets: Put the point on each mark
teach.note: Model one petal first. Check pupils are keeping the compass width the same.

teach.heading: Colouring with care
teach.note: Neatness is part of excellence (ihsan in work). Encourage pupils to colour in one direction.

practice: How many petals will our flower have?
Draw a square with a ruler.
independent: Draw the circle and mark six points around it.
Draw the six arcs through the centre to make the flower.
exit: Complete and colour your six-petal flower.
Draw a second flower overlapping the first to start a pattern.
homework: Why must the compass width stay the same?
lessons.send: Draw a six-petal flower at home and add colour.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: What is a mosaic?
lessons.bigQuestion: Some mosaics are nearly 2,000 years old and still bright. What makes them last so long?
objectives: To understand what a mosaic is and how small pieces (tesserae) make patterns and pictures
successCriteria: Most: describe the pattern in a Roman or Islamic mosaic
Some: explain why mosaics last for hundreds of years
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Roman Britain (Year 3 Tribal Tales and Rome)
lessons.smsc: Cultural: mosaics in Roman Britain and in Islamic architecture

keywords.def: a picture or pattern made of small pieces
the small pieces in a mosaic

hook.text: Some mosaics are nearly 2,000 years old and still bright. What makes them last so long?
hook.a: Stone, glass and tile pieces do not fade like paint, and they are set firmly in the floor or wall.

islamicLink.text: The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus (built about 715 CE) has huge golden mosaics of trees, rivers and buildings, with no people or animals: Muslim artists showed beauty through nature and pattern.

teach.heading: Tiny pieces, big picture
bullets: Tesserae: small squares of stone, glass or tile
teach.note: Show a close-up of tesserae.

teach.heading: Two traditions
teach.note: Photos of geometric and plant designs only.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: The small pieces in a mosaic
check.why: Tesserae are the tiles that make a mosaic.

practice.q: Look at the geometric Roman border photo. Describe the repeating pattern.
practice.a: For example: a wave shape repeating along the border in black and white.
practice.model: I do: I see a black square, then a white square, repeating, like a chessboard border.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: on squared paper, colour a 10 by 10 square border pattern using 3 colours, like a Roman border.
independent.a: A neat repeating border in 3 colours.
independent.model: The teacher colours the first two repeats.

independent.q: Extend: write two sentences comparing Roman and masjid mosaics.
independent.a: Roman ones often have geometric borders; masjid ones show trees and buildings in gold.

exit.a: stone and glass do not fade
options: stone and glass do not fade

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Some mosaics are nearly 2,000 years old and still bright. What makes them last so long?
exit.a: Stone, glass and tile pieces do not fade like paint, and they are set firmly in the floor or wall.

lessons.homework: Find a repeating pattern at home (tiles, fabric, a rug) and sketch it.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: Colour and pattern: designing a mosaic
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you think many Islamic patterns use symmetry?
objectives: To understand how to plan a geometric or plant mosaic using a colour scheme and symmetry
successCriteria: All: draw a simple design on squared paper
Most: use a colour scheme of three or four colours
Some: use symmetry or repetition on purpose
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order and beauty in creation

keywords.def: both halves match like a mirror
made of shapes like squares and triangles
a plan for something you will make

hook.text: Why do you think many Islamic patterns use symmetry?
hook.a: Symmetry gives balance and order, reflecting the order in Allah's creation.

islamicLink.text: Allah is the One 'Who perfected everything which He created' (As-Sajdah 32:7). Muslim artists use balance and symmetry to reflect this order.

starter.a: The Umayyad Mosque, Damascus; Fishbourne Roman Palace.

teach.heading: Choose a colour scheme
bullets: Repeat colours to link the design

teach.heading: Symmetry
teach.note: Fold a paper square to show a mirror line.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: both halves match like a mirror

practice.q: Complete the other half of the symmetrical flower on the slide.
practice.a: A mirror image of the half flower.
practice.model: I do: count the squares from the mirror line and copy each one across.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: design your own mosaic (geometric or a plant) on a 16 by 16 grid with a colour key.
independent.a: A symmetrical design with a 3 to 4 colour key.
independent.model: The teacher draws a star border design.

independent.q: Extend: write why you chose your colours.
independent.a: For example: 'Blue and gold, like the masjid mosaics.'

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why do you think many Islamic patterns use symmetry?
exit.a: Symmetry gives balance and order, reflecting the order in Allah's creation.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: Making a paper mosaic
lessons.bigQuestion: What would happen if all the pieces touched with no gaps at all?
objectives: To understand how to cut, arrange and stick paper tesserae with even gaps to make my mosaic
successCriteria: All: cut paper squares of similar size
Most: stick pieces with small, even gaps
Some: follow my design closely and evaluate it
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience and care (itqan) in making

hook.text: What would happen if all the pieces touched with no gaps at all?
hook.a: It would look like one block of colour; the gaps show the tesserae and make it look like a mosaic.

starter.q: How many colours in your scheme?

teach.heading: Safety first
teach.note: Short week: 40 minutes of making; finish at home.

teach.heading: Cut and sort
cycle: Glue a small area at a time

misconception.wrong: Gluing the whole page first and dropping pieces anywhere
misconception.right: Glue small areas and place pieces one by one with even gaps

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Why glue a small area at a time?
options: The glue does not dry before you place pieces
It is faster to make a mess

practice.q: Watch the teacher place the first row. What size gap is left?
practice.a: About 1 to 2 mm, the same each time.
practice.model: I do: glue a 3 cm patch, place squares in a row, leaving a thin even gap.

independent.q: Make your mosaic from your design (finish at home if needed); photograph and upload it.
independent.a: A paper mosaic with even gaps following the design.
independent.model: The teacher completes one corner on camera.

independent.q: Extend: write one thing that went well and one to improve.
independent.a: For example: 'Even gaps; next time smaller pieces for curves.'

exit.q: Back to our ponder: What would happen if all the pieces touched with no gaps at all?
exit.a: It would look like one block of colour; the gaps show the tesserae and make it look like a mosaic.

lessons.homework: Finish your mosaic and upload a photo.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: DT: designing a woven basket
lessons.bigQuestion: Before plastic, how did people carry and store food?
objectives: To understand how Iron Age and Celtic people wove containers and how to design a paper-strip basket that meets criteria
successCriteria: Most: write design criteria for my basket
Some: label a design with sizes and materials
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Iron Age Britain and the Celts (Tribal Tales)

keywords.def: pass strips over and under each other
the strips that go one way and stay still

hook.text: Before plastic, how did people carry and store food?
hook.a: Woven baskets, clay pots, leather bags: made by hand from natural materials.

starter.q: Name one thing that went well in your mosaic.

teach.heading: Baskets in the Iron Age
teach.note: Show photos of woven baskets (objects only).

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: across, over and under the warp
check.why: Weft is woven across the warp.

practice.q: Write one design criterion for strength.
practice.a: 'It must hold a small orange without bending.'
practice.model: I do: 'The base must stay flat when I put a satsuma in.'

independent.q: Pupil PDF: design your basket: draw it from the front and above, label sizes, materials and colours, and list three criteria.
independent.a: A labelled design with three criteria.
independent.model: The teacher labels the base: card square 10 cm.

independent.q: Extend: why would a tight weave be stronger?
independent.a: Strips support each other with fewer gaps.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Before plastic, how did people carry and store food?
exit.a: Woven baskets, clay pots, leather bags: made by hand from natural materials.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: DT: making and testing the basket
lessons.bigQuestion: How could you make paper strong enough to carry something?
objectives: To understand how to make a woven basket from a card base and paper strips and test it against my criteria
successCriteria: All: weave strips over and under
Most: fold the warp up to make sides and weave around
Some: test with light items and record the result
lessons.smsc: Moral: perseverance when making something difficult

keywords.def: a long thin piece of paper

hook.text: How could you make paper strong enough to carry something?
hook.a: Folding it, weaving it so strips support each other, and gluing the ends.

teach.heading: Make the base
teach.note: Model on camera.

teach.heading: Tips
bullets: Paper clips hold strips while drying

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: To make the second row, you start ...
options: under, if the first row started over
the same as the first row

practice.q: Watch the teacher weave two rows. Why does row 2 start under?
practice.a: So it locks the strips and does not slide.
practice.model: I do: row 1 over, under, over...; row 2 under, over, under...

independent.q: Make your basket (finish at home if needed), test with three items and record results on the pupil PDF.
independent.a: A finished basket and a results table.
independent.model: The teacher finishes the first two rows of weft.

independent.q: Extend: suggest one change to make it stronger.
independent.a: Use card strips for the warp; weave tighter.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: How could you make paper strong enough to carry something?
exit.a: Folding it, weaving it so strips support each other, and gluing the ends.

lessons.homework: Finish and test your basket; upload a photo.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Mosaics and woven baskets (Mosaic Masters and Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: Evaluate: basket and mosaic
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a 'failed' test a waste of time?
objectives: To understand how to evaluate my work against the criteria and suggest improvements
successCriteria: All: say whether each criterion was met
Most: give evidence from my test
Some: suggest a specific improvement and why it would work
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest self-assessment and kind feedback

hook.text: Is a 'failed' test a waste of time?
hook.a: No: it shows what to change. Good designers learn from every test.

starter.q: Did your basket hold a satsuma?

teach.heading: Class gallery
bullets: Peers give one star and one wish

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: 'It held 2 satsumas; next time a card warp for more strength'

practice.q: Write one evaluation sentence with evidence.
practice.a: 'My basket stood up and held one satsuma, but bent with two.'
practice.model: I do: criterion, result, evidence: 'It was neat: my rows were tight with no gaps.'

independent.q: Pupil PDF: evaluate the basket and the mosaic (two short paragraphs) and give a star and a wish to two classmates in the chat.
independent.a: Two evaluations with evidence and improvements; two peer comments.
independent.model: The teacher evaluates a sample basket.

independent.q: Extend: which project did you enjoy most, and why?

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Is a 'failed' test a waste of time?
exit.a: No: it shows what to change. Good designers learn from every test.

lessons.homework: Show your family your basket and mosaic and explain one improvement.
